key_claim: Farming let humans build bigger societies and even writing, but early farmers often had worse health than hunter-gatherers.

slides.headline: Farming changed everything. Not always for the better.
It began in many places at once
slides.body: About 12,000 years ago, people in several parts of the world started growing food. Each region worked it out on its own.

slides.headline: More food, worse health
slides.body: Farming fed far more people. But early farmers were often shorter, had worse teeth and caught more diseases than hunter-gatherers.

slides.headline: Its strangest legacy? Writing.
slides.body: Around 3200 BCE, Sumerians began writing to track grain and taxes. Many early tablets just count barley and beer.

figure.title: Writing came thousands of years after farming

slides.headline: Civilisation started with a trade-off.
slides.body: More food. Bigger societies. A new set of problems.

caption:
Farming changed everything. Not always for the better.

Around 12,000 years ago, humans began growing food, independently in multiple parts of the world.

The payoff? Larger populations and, eventually, complex civilisations.

The catch? Early farmers often had worse health than hunter-gatherers.

And one of farming's surprising legacies? Writing. Some of the earliest written records tracked goods like grain and beer.

Three reminders that progress is rarely as simple as it looks.

Source: Waypoint — The Agricultural Revolution
